text: 64 patterns for exploration, progress, and continuous improvement.
The I Ching describes change through 64 hexagrams—patterns of emergence, discovery, resistance, cooperation, transformation, and renewal.
At Hanzo, we use these patterns as inspiration for building intelligent systems and advancing research.
Science progresses by asking questions, challenging assumptions, testing ideas, learning from failure, and discovering what becomes possible next.
Intelligence grows through that same process.
Eight categories. Sixty-four perspectives. Infinite possibilities for discovery.

These are modern Hanzo interpretations inspired by the I Ching, not claims about the text’s historical or scientific meaning. The eight categories are Hanzo’s own editorial grouping of the hexagrams in King Wen order.
Generate new possibilities. Imagine what does not yet exist, then seek a way to test it.
Sketch an architecture or training objective nobody has tried, and write down the result that would show it works.
State a new hypothesis in a form an experiment can refute.
Set aside time for proposals that have no owner yet, then pick a few to test.
Curiosity, possibility, and the beginning of discovery
Every breakthrough begins with a question. Exploration requires imagination, openness, uncertainty, and the willingness to venture beyond what is already understood.
Receive evidence without forcing it to fit existing expectations.
Begin productive work amid uncertainty. Establish the first usable foundations.
Recognize what is unknown. Ask questions before assuming answers.
Gather evidence, establish readiness, and recognize when conditions support action.
Investigate competing explanations. Use disagreement to reveal hidden assumptions.
Organize people, agents, knowledge, and resources around a shared objective.
Connect complementary capabilities and align participants around common evidence.
Ideas become useful when they acquire structure. Formation transforms possibilities into methods, systems, experiments, and coordinated research programs.
Make small, measurable improvements before attempting larger changes.
Proceed with discipline, understand the risks, and respect experimental boundaries.
Align objectives, methods, resources, and interfaces so progress can flow.
Recognize stagnation. Identify what prevents learning or execution.
Advance knowledge through shared methods, open inquiry, and collaboration.
Manage abundant knowledge, compute, talent, and resources responsibly.
Distinguish confidence from certainty. Remain willing to revise conclusions.
Convert promising ideas into coordinated initiatives with clear goals.
Progress depends on the ability to see reality clearly. Observation connects hypotheses to evidence and makes errors visible before they become embedded in systems.
Follow reliable evidence when it leads somewhere unexpected.
Identify outdated assumptions, faulty methods, and accumulated technical debt.
Make complex systems, tools, and findings understandable and usable.
Study behavior carefully before attempting to change it.
Confront inconsistencies directly. Resolve questions with explicit tests and evidence.
Make discoveries legible through clear models, figures, interfaces, and explanations.
Break complex problems into components that can be independently examined.
Return to reference conditions, repeat experiments, and establish reliable baselines.
Experiments transform possibilities into evidence. Robust research requires trustworthy inputs, controlled execution, transparent measurements, and resilience when reality differs from prediction.
Test hypotheses without manipulating the conditions to favor an expected outcome.
Develop the instruments, models, datasets, and computational capacity needed for difficult investigations.
Recognize that the reliability of results depends on the quality of evidence, data, and inputs.
Explore extreme conditions and discover where existing methods fail.
Investigate uncertainty, repeated failures, and adverse conditions without losing the research record.
Illuminate internal behavior through instrumentation, diagnostics, and interpretable measurements.
Investigate relationships, feedback, dependencies, and possible causal mechanisms.
Test whether findings remain reliable across time, environments, and changing conditions.
Constraints, resistance, changing conditions, and new directions
Research rarely proceeds exactly as planned. Adaptation is the ability to recognize limitations, reconsider assumptions, and change direction without losing what has already been learned.
Stop unproductive investigations when evidence no longer justifies their cost.
Apply powerful tools with appropriate limits, safeguards, and oversight.
Establish whether a new method represents a genuine improvement over its baseline.
Protect sensitive discoveries, research participants, confidential data, and intellectual property.
Establish clear ownership, trusted collaboration, and accountable research groups.
Explore alternative models, contradictory observations, and competing theories.
Identify the physical, computational, organizational, or methodological limitation preventing progress.
Remove unnecessary constraints and restore the ability to investigate and experiment.
Efficiency, leverage, experimental value, and shared foundations
Research resources are finite. Optimization seeks better results through intelligent allocation of time, compute, energy, capital, instruments, and human attention.
Remove unnecessary complexity while preserving essential scientific capability.
Identify improvements that amplify productivity across many experiments or systems.
Make consequential choices when evidence satisfies defined criteria.
Evaluate unexpected discoveries, emerging methods, and external innovations before integrating them.
Bring complementary datasets, tools, expertise, and discoveries into a coherent research system.
Extend validated methods to larger problems without losing correctness or efficiency.
Continue useful investigation under limited compute, funding, time, or experimental capacity.
Build reusable scientific foundations that support many researchers and disciplines.
New methods, synthesis, deployment, and transformation
Discovery changes what is possible. Transformation converts established knowledge into new architectures, research methods, technologies, and practical capabilities.
Replace an established approach when stronger evidence supports a fundamentally better alternative.
Combine methods and insights from different disciplines to create new capabilities.
Respond constructively to unexpected findings, anomalies, or sudden changes.
Pause when additional investigation, independent review, or stronger controls are required.
Build understanding through successive refinements and validated milestones.
Examine compatibility, hidden dependencies, and unintended consequences when combining systems.
Extract meaningful findings from abundant observations, experiments, and possibilities.
Move methods and knowledge between laboratories, disciplines, hardware, and organizations.
Dissemination, verification, maturity, and continuous becoming
Every result changes the conditions for future research. Evolution turns discoveries into shared knowledge, mature capabilities, and new questions.
Spread useful capabilities through reusable, interoperable methods and components.
Advance understanding through reciprocal learning, constructive criticism, and open dialogue.
Enable independent researchers and institutions to contribute to a larger body of knowledge.
Use explicit limits and standards to make research safer, clearer, and more reproducible.
Ground claims in traceable observations, documented methods, and reproducible analysis.
Refine small details whose effects can determine scientific or engineering success.
Preserve reliability through validation, monitoring, maintenance, and disciplined change.
Recognize that every answer creates new questions and every achievement opens new possibilities.
A model can become more capable. An experiment can reveal a better question. A failed hypothesis can redirect an entire research program. A discovery in one discipline can transform another.
Progress is not a straight line, and intelligence is not a fixed destination.
These 64 patterns provide different perspectives for recognizing the condition of a problem and choosing how to proceed.
The same principles can inform the development of an AI model, a scientific experiment, a research laboratory, an organization, or an evolving technological ecosystem.
Explore. Form. Observe. Experiment. Adapt. Optimize. Transform. Evolve.
